transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my family really pushed me to come in and talk to someone. It's about my father's death. 

I know everyone keeps telling me that the hospital records and the donation emails all line up perfectly. But... I look at data and systems for a living. When I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, the missing attachments in those emails, and... just the way certain community members completely avoid my questions when I bring it up, it’s obvious to me. 

Someone is hiding what really happened around his death. People keep saying I'm just having a hard time letting go, but the information right in front of me says otherwise.

Before your father passed away, would you say you typically analyzed information and noticed patterns the way you're describing now, or does this level of detailed scrutiny of data and people's behavior feel like something newer for you?

Well, I mean... I've always been analytical. I'm a systems analyst, so looking at data, finding patterns, noticing when things don't match up... that's just what I do for a living. I've always been like that with information. 

But as far as looking at people's behavior... I don't know. I'm not really sure if I scrutinized things quite like this before. I guess I haven't really thought about whether it's new. I'm just trying to make sense of what I'm seeing right now.
When did you first start having these concerns about what really happened to your father? Was it right after he died, or did it develop over time?

It's been going on for about nine months now. It didn't happen the exact day he passed, but... it started in the period right after he died, when I had to sit down and start sorting through his records and messages. That's when I actually started looking at the data and realized things weren't adding up.

How much of your time each day would you say you're spending thinking about or investigating what happened with your father's death? And has this affected your ability to work, sleep, or do other things you normally do?

I'd say I spend a fair bit of time looking into it, but it hasn't really stopped me from doing what I need to do. I still go to work every day, handle my projects, pay my bills... I keep my normal routine just fine. It hasn't affected my sleep or my job performance at all. 

Really, the main place things get tense is just... well, when I bring up my questions about my father's records with my family, or with certain community members. They don't want to hear it, and that's where the friction is. But as far as my daily responsibilities go, everything is completely normal.

If someone you trusted completely - like a family member or authority figure - sat down and walked you through all the hospital records and email timestamps point by point and explained how they actually do line up, would that change your mind about what happened, or do you think there's still something being hidden that they're either not seeing or not telling you?

I mean... I hear what you're asking. And I know everyone keeps telling me that the hospital records and those donation emails all line up. But even if someone I trusted went through it with me point by point... no, I don't think it would change my mind. 

Because I've looked at the data myself. When I compare the timestamps, and I see the missing attachments... it just doesn't match the official story. And it's not just the files. It's the way certain community members completely avoid my questions when I ask for basic clarification. It’s just obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. So even if someone else doesn't see it, or if they're just not telling me... I know what I'm looking at.

If you were to discover tomorrow that you had made an error in your analysis of those timestamps - that you had misread or misunderstood the data - how would you react to that? Do you think that's possible, or are you completely certain that your interpretation is correct?

I don't think that's possible. I mean, I do this for a living. I analyze systems and data every single day. I know how to read timestamps and track digital footprints. 

I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly. But I've looked at them. When I compare the timestamps on those emails to the time of death, and look at the missing attachments... it just doesn't make sense. And it's not just the digital side of it. It's the way certain community members completely avoid my questions or change the subject when I try to get basic answers. 

So, no, I'm completely certain my interpretation is correct. It's just obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father's death. I haven't made an error.
Have you experienced anything unusual with your senses - like hearing voices, seeing things, or sensing things that others around you don't seem to notice or can't explain?

No, nothing like that. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. My senses are completely normal. I mean... I'm just looking at the actual data and the emails, like I said. There's nothing wrong with my hearing or my vision, I'm just paying attention to the facts in front of me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a circumscribed, non-bizarre delusional belief system centered on the conviction that his father's death was concealed, persisting for 9 months despite contradictory evidence and lack of functional impairment. Key diagnostic features include: (1) fixed false belief resistant to correction by trusted authority figures or logical evidence; (2) belief based on misinterpretation of real data (timestamps, emails) rather than bizarre or implausible content; (3) no hallucinations or other psychotic symptoms; (4) preserved functioning in work, sleep, and daily responsibilities; (5) minimal impact on occupational or social functioning except interpersonal tension when discussing the belief. This constellation is consistent with Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22.0). The significant psychosocial stressor (father's death) and 9-month timeline could suggest Adjustment Disorder with Disturbance of Emotions and Conduct (F43.10), but the fixed, unshakeable nature of the belief and resistance to reality-testing by trusted figures exceeds what would be expected in adjustment disorder and points more definitively toward a primary delusional disorder.
